title: The conquest of Mecca
hookLine: the Prophet ﷺ enters Mecca with ten thousand, almost without fighting, head bowed

cards: Years ago, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ slipped out of Mecca by night, hunted, with a price on his head. He looked back at the city and said he loved it, and would never have left if its people hadn't driven him out.

Now it's Ramadan again. Mecca's allies have broken the peace of Hudaybiyyah, attacking a tribe allied to the Muslims. One night the people of Mecca look out from the hills and see the valley below covered in campfires.
The army behind them is ten thousand strong. The man they drove out has come back, and everyone in the city knows what conquerors do.

teach.h: ABU SUFYAN WATCHES THE ARMY PASS.
teach.b: That night, Abu Sufyan, Mecca's leader and the Prophet's old enemy, came out to see the camp, and before the army entered he had become Muslim.
Sahih al-Bukhari says he was made to stand at a narrow pass and watch the army file by, tribe after tribe, until the Prophet's own company came past.
And the Prophet sent him back to the city with an offer, recorded in Sahih Muslim: whoever enters Abu Sufyan's house is safe.

teach.h: WHOEVER SHUTS HIS DOOR IS SAFE.
teach.b: Whoever shuts his own door is safe. Whoever enters the Sacred Mosque is safe. As the columns moved in, one commander, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, called out that today was the day of slaughter.

teach.h: A DAY TO HONOR THE KAABA.
teach.b: Bukhari says the Prophet answered that Sa'd had it wrong: this is a day on which God will honor the Kaaba.

The early biographers add that he took the banner from Sa'd, and they remember the reply as: today is the day of mercy. There was a brief clash on one side of the city. Otherwise, Mecca was entered almost without a fight.
The biographers describe him riding in on his camel with his head bowed so low, in humility before God, that his beard nearly touched the saddle.

A companion in Sahih al-Bukhari remembered him reciting Surah al-Fath, the Victory, as he rode, softly, his voice wavering over the sounds: the surah that came after Hudaybiyyah, when it all looked like losing.
He had left this city hunted, at night. He came back with its gates open, and he came back bowing.

how: Muslims remember the conquest of Mecca, in Ramadan, as the moment the Kaaba was cleared of idols and returned to the worship of one God, and it's often told as a lesson in humility and mercy in victory.

games.q: you've come back with ten thousand to the city that drove you out. one of your commanders shouts: today is the day of slaughter. what do you do?
o: take the banner and say: today is the day of mercy.
games.why: Bukhari says he answered: this is a day on which God will honor the Kaaba. the biographers add: today is the day of mercy.

practice: Picture the next room you'll walk into where you have some standing: your team, your family, a class you teach, a place where people wait on your word.
Picture yourself walking in the way the Prophet rode into Mecca: head a little lowered, voice soft, taking up no more space than you need. If you pray, you can remember that every win is God's.

wordCard.voice: Abu Sufyan, Mecca's old leader who became Muslim the night before the Prophet's return with ten thousand, almost without fighting.

orig.note: Arabic: the opening of Mecca. fath, the same word as al-Fath, the Victory.

carryVoice: Your line: head bowed on the camel. Even a win can be received quietly. Until tomorrow.
